newsitem.title: FRANCE: Arthuis says early poll will boost economy.
newsitem.headline: Arthuis says early poll will boost economy.

text.p: French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said on Monday a snap general election would help dispel investor uncertainty and cut the country's record 12.8 percent unemployment.

He denied media reports that parliamentary elections, expected to be announced later on Monday by President Jacques Chirac, nine months ahead of schedule, were linked to a need for radical new austerity measures to help France qualify for European monetary union.
"To have jobs, we need growth. Certainly, the situation is improving" he said, pointing to expectations that the economy would grow by a minimum 2.3 percent in 1997 and 2.8 percent next year.

"But what we need now is investment and it's well known investors are reluctant to invest before an election so if we want these key factors behind growth and jobs, it would be better to speed up the electoral calendar," he said.

He said the centre-right government was committed to keeping a lid on public spending but, when asked about media reports tough new measures would be needed to ensure France met the criteria for monetary union, he replied: "This is nonsense."
"Public finances are under control," he told a news conference at which designs were unveiled for the French version of the new euro coins.

He added there was no truth to reports that social security contributions to finance the welfare system would have to be raised to cut public deficits in time for monetary union, due to go into effect on January 1, 1999.

Election talk was stoked last week by a leaked Finance Ministry memo which painted a "worst-case" scenario of a deficit of 3.8 percent of gross domestic product this year, ballooning to 4.5 percent next year, mainly due to an overshoot on the social security deficit.
European countries wishing to qualify for monetary union, due to start on January 1, 1999, must cut their budget deficits to three percent of gross domestic product in 1997.

Chirac is reportedly reluctant to call the polls next spring, when countries qualifying for a single currency are due to be chosen, because he fears electoral unhappiness over spending cuts could turn the vote into a politically risky referendum on monetary union.
Arthuis side-stepped questions over whether an early election could backfire on the government when unemployment is so high. The government now has 478 of the National Assembly's 577 seats.

"We need five more years to pursue and enlarge the structural reforms of the state...and to clean up public finances," he said, saying the previous Socialist administration had left behind a "calamitous record."
Economists said an early election could benefit financial markets by resulting in a tighter 1998 budget.
"It is quite obvious we would not get a tight budget if the parliamentary elections were held next March," said Marie Owens-Thomsen of BIP.
A poll in the newspaper Le Figaro suggested the centre-right coalition would lose 150 seats but keep a comfortable majority.
